title: What Distinguishes the Persons?

keyTerms.d: The tradition’s precise answer to what distinguishes the persons: they are distinguished from one another by nothing except who is from whom. The Father is unbegotten, from no one (paternity); the Son is eternally begotten of the Father (filiation); the Spirit eternally proceeds (procession). In everything that belongs to being God — eternity, power, wisdom, goodness, will, the one undivided essence — the three are utterly identical and fully equal; they differ solely in the relation each bears to the others. A relation of origin is never an inequality: the persons are distinguished by order, never by rank.

The Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed’s confession that the Son is “of one substance with the Father” — the same being, not a similar one — “begotten, not made… God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God.” The Athanasian Creed states the balance the three rules protect: we worship one God in Trinity, “neither confounding the persons” (modalism) “nor dividing the substance” (tritheism).

The mutual indwelling of the persons (Latin circumincessio): each is wholly in the others, cleaving to one another without being confused, compounded, or mingled. Given its classic Trinitarian use by John of Damascus. It is not a blurring — a thing cannot indwell itself — so it takes real distinction for indwelling to mean anything at all; it manifests the unity the one essence grounds and forbids any picture of three separate beings, without manufacturing a oneness out of three that would otherwise stand apart.

Opera Trinitatis ad extra indivisa sunt — the outward works of the Trinity are undivided. In every act directed outside the Godhead — creating, sustaining, redeeming, sanctifying — the three persons act not as three agents dividing the labor but as the one God, from a single power and will. The maxim is traceable to Augustine and standard in East and West alike.

Why Scripture can assign a particular work to a particular person — creation to the Father, redemption to the Son, sanctification to the Spirit — without dividing the work. A work common to all three is attributed by special affinity to the person whose relation of origin it most fits, so as to reveal the persons to us. Appropriation divides the naming, never the working: the Father does not create while the Son waits; all three create, and creation shows us the Father.

Thomas Aquinas’s sharpest formulation: a divine person just is a subsistent relation — the relation of paternity, filiation, or procession, existing as a hypostasis. In creatures a relation is an accident added to a substance; but in God, who is utterly simple, the relation is really identical with the essence yet really distinct from its opposing relation. The persons are not three things that happen to stand in relations; the relation is the person.

The Western addition of “and the Son” to the creed’s statement that the Spirit “proceeds from the Father”; the Christian East retained the original wording and objected to the addition. A genuine and ancient East–West disagreement about the ordering of the Spirit’s relation of origin, which Apologia Daily reports rather than settles. Both traditions confess, without reservation, the full, co-equal, co-eternal deity of the Holy Spirit; the dispute is about the grammar of procession, never about whether the Spirit is God.

keyTerms.t: The logical problem of the Trinity
keyTerms.d: The charge, framed by Richard Cartwright and pressed by the unitarian philosopher Dale Tuggy, that taken as ordinary identity statements the creed says the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Father is not the Son — formally contradictory unless “is God” means something other than strict identity. The reply locates the equivocation: the persons are not each identical to the essence as one thing is identical to another; they are the one essence subsisting in three relationally distinct ways.

derive.q: The more seriously we mean that the three persons are co-equal and co-eternal — sharing every divine attribute without remainder — the sharper one question gets. Which one?
derive.ans: what is left over to distinguish them at all
derive.why: This is not the beginner’s question (how can three be one?) but the advanced one, and it is far sharper. For the more truly the three persons are one in essence — truly co-equal, sharing every divine attribute without remainder — the more urgent it becomes to say what distinguishes them at all.

derive.q: Name no real difference and the persons collapse into three masks of one God. Name a difference of attribute, rank, or will and you have three gods. So the distinction the tradition needs must be…?
derive.ans: real enough to escape modalism, slight enough to escape tritheism
derive.why: The whole art of Trinitarian theology is to find a distinction real enough to escape the first cliff (modalism) and slight enough to escape the second (tritheism). The tradition’s answer is not one clever move but three disciplined rules — relations of origin, perichoresis, inseparable operations — that together do exactly that.

derive.q: The Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten, the Spirit proceeding. These name who-is-from-whom, not who-is-greater. So the one and only difference between the persons is…?
derive.ans: their relation of origin — never their rank
derive.why: What distinguishes the Father from the Son is not that one is more divine, or wills something the other does not, or holds an attribute the other lacks — there is no such difference and can be none. It is simply that the Father eternally gives, and the Son eternally receives, the one whole divine life. That is the entire distinction: real, yet relational — a distinction of order, never of rank.

derive.q: “For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:26). The Son has the very self-existence of God — yet has it as granted, eternally received from the Father. So derivation of the person is…?
derive.why: This is precisely where Arianism went wrong, reasoning that if the Son is begotten he must have had a beginning and so be a creature, secondary and lesser. Nicaea refused the inference: “begotten, not made… true God from true God.” Being from the Father is the Son’s glory, not his demotion; the radiance is exactly as old and exactly as bright as the flame. Derivation of person is not inequality of essence; the three are co-equal and co-eternal.

derive.q: Relations of origin might still leave you picturing three individuals lined up like points on a line — source, begotten, proceeding. What one rule forbids that picture?
derive.ans: perichoresis — each person wholly in the others
derive.why: The persons do not stand outside one another; each is wholly in the others (John 14:10–11). They are not three separate beings side by side, cooperating like a good committee; each is so fully in the others that where one is, all are. Perichoresis manifests the unity the one essence grounds and forbids any picture of three separate beings — it does not manufacture that oneness.

derive.q: Grant all three rules, held together. Do they dissolve the mystery, or prove the Trinity to a skeptic?
derive.ans: neither — they are rules for right speech, not a proof or a diagram
derive.why: It would betray the tradition to present these rules as though they dispelled the mystery; they are disciplined rules for speech, not a diagram of the divine interior, and they hand no one a proof that would compel a skeptic. They are the confession of those who already worship the triune God, spelling out how that worship holds together without contradiction.

honestState.p1: What the three rules establish is bounded, and the essay says so plainly: they are disciplined rules for right speech, not a diagram of the divine interior. Together they secure a real, permanent, three-fold distinction of the persons (against modalism) and an unbreakable unity (against tritheism) — distinction without division, unity without confusion. What they do not do is dispel the mystery: the how of eternal generation — the Father communicating the whole divine life to the Son without time, change, or division — remains incomprehensible, and we possess no positive model that makes it transparent. The claim is only the modest one — that no contradiction has been demonstrated.
honestState.fairness: The coherence question is pressed hardest by the unitarian philosopher Dale Tuggy (the persons are either too thin to be real persons or too thick to be one God) and, decades earlier, by Richard Cartwright (read as identity statements, the creed looks formally contradictory). From within the household of faith, Cornelius Plantinga and the “social” stream of Trinitarian thought worry that the classical relations-and-simplicity account makes the persons so thin that it drifts toward modalism. Apologia Daily does not adjudicate the intramural debate between social and classical Trinitarians as a whole — both camps intend full Nicene orthodoxy, and each accuses the other of leaning toward the opposite cliff — nor the East–West dispute over the Filioque; both are reported, not settled.
honestState.verdict: So the actual difference between the Father, the Son, and the Spirit is nothing in nature, power, will, eternity, or worth — in all of that they are one and equal — but one of relation and origin alone: the Father unbegotten, the Son eternally begotten, the Spirit eternally proceeding, each wholly indwelling the others, all working every work as one God. The precision is the point: it says just enough to make the persons genuinely distinct (against modalism) and not one syllable more that would make them genuinely separate (against tritheism). These rules do not prove the Trinity or compel a skeptic; they are the confession of those who already worship the triune God. The positive case rests on revelation and on who Jesus showed himself to be — and what it guards is that God is eternally relational: Father, Son, and Spirit, giving, receiving, and indwelling, in a communion with no beginning.

order: The three persons share one essence, one will, one power — co-equal and co-eternal in every divine attribute; so whatever distinguishes them cannot be a difference of nature, degree, or rank.
Yet the persons are really and eternally distinct — the Father is not the Son is not the Spirit; paternity, filiation, and procession are irreducible (against modalism’s three masks).

Therefore the only distinction is relation of origin — who is from whom; perichoresis (mutual indwelling) and inseparable operations, resting on the one essence, manifest the unity against tritheism, and the real, eternal relations secure the distinction against modalism.

props.t: a real, eternal distinction of the persons — the Father is not the Son
the one difference is relation of origin — who is from whom
a relation of origin is never an inequality — order, not rank
perichoresis: each person wholly in the others, one God
inseparable operations: the three act as one agent
appropriation reveals a person, it never divides the work
only the Son became incarnate — the undivided act terminates in the Son alone
dispels the mystery and lets us picture the difference between the persons
proves the Trinity to a skeptic from these three rules alone
settles the Filioque dispute between East and West
ranks the persons as a hierarchy of being — begotten means lesser
makes each person a distinct centre of will and power
shows that the divine nature itself suffered and died on the cross

cards.q: State Premise 1 — and its precision check.
cards.a: The three persons share one essence, one will, one power — co-equal and co-eternal in every divine attribute. Precision: in everything that belongs to being God — eternity, power, wisdom, goodness, will, the one undivided essence — the three are utterly identical and fully equal. So whatever distinguishes them cannot be a difference of nature, degree, or rank.

cards.q: State Premise 2 — and its precision check.
cards.a: Yet the persons are really and eternally distinct — the Father is not the Son is not the Spirit. Precision: the distinction is real — paternity is not filiation, and no theology can make the Father be the Son — yet relational, not a distinction of nature. Paternity, filiation, and procession are eternal and irreducible, which is exactly what rules out modalism.

cards.q: What does the conclusion reach — and not reach?
cards.a: That the only distinction is relation of origin (who is from whom), so the persons are genuinely distinct (against modalism) and genuinely one God (against tritheism). It does not dispel the mystery, hand over a diagram of the divine interior, or prove the Trinity to a skeptic; it is the confession of those who already worship the triune God.

cards.q: What is the one difference between the persons — and what is it not?
cards.a: It is their relation of origin: the Father unbegotten, the Son eternally begotten, the Spirit eternally proceeding — who is from whom. It is NOT a difference of nature, power, will, eternity, or worth; in all of that they are one and equal. The difference is of order, never of rank.

cards.q: Why is a relation of origin not an inequality?
cards.a: Because it orders the persons without grading the essence. Nicaea refused the Arian inference that begotten means later and later means lesser: the Son is “begotten, not made… true God from true God.” He receives not a portion or a lower grade but the whole undivided divine life, given wholly. The radiance is exactly as old and exactly as bright as the flame.

cards.q: What does perichoresis do — and not do?
cards.a: Mutual indwelling: each person is wholly IN the others (John 14:10–11), so they are never three beings side by side. It MANIFESTS the unity the one essence grounds and forbids the picture of three separate beings; it does not MANUFACTURE a oneness out of three. Nor does it collapse them — a thing cannot indwell itself, so indwelling presupposes real distinction.

cards.q: Inseparable operations — and the one marked exception?
cards.a: In every outward act the three persons work as one agent, from a single power and will (John 5:19), not three agents dividing the labor. The one exception: only the Son became incarnate. The whole Trinity works the one act of the incarnation, but its term — the person in whom human nature subsists — is proper to the Son alone.

cards.q: What does “appropriation” mean — and what must it never do?
cards.a: A work common to all three — creation, redemption, sanctification — is attributed by special affinity to the one person whose relation of origin it most fits, so as to reveal the persons. It must never divide the work: appropriation divides the naming, never the working. The Father does not create while the Son waits; all three create, and creation shows us the Father.

cards.q: Reply to: “Father is God, Son is God, Father is not the Son — that is a flat contradiction.”
cards.a: Only if “is God” meant numerical identity between person and essence — then both, being identical to the one essence, would have to be identical to each other. But the persons are not each identical to the essence as one thing to another; they are the one essence subsisting in three relationally distinct ways. Opposed relations (paternity, filiation) differ from each other without either differing from the essence — so the Father is distinct from the Son, but neither is distinct from the Godhead. Not the same respect; no contradiction.

cards.q: Reply to Tuggy’s dilemma — the persons are too thin (modalism) or too thick (tritheism)?
cards.a: The dilemma omits perichoresis and the one will. The one who thinks, loves, and acts is not a bare relation but the divine essence itself, subsisting as this relationally distinct person — acting in the one undivided operation of the one God, not as three separate minds. Conceded plainly: we have no positive model making the HOW transparent. The claim is only that no contradiction has been demonstrated.

cards.q: On the cross, who suffered — and in what nature? (the fence that keeps inseparable operations orthodox)
cards.a: The incarnate Son truly suffered and died, in the human nature he assumed; because only the Son became man, the cross is properly his. NOT the divine nature itself (the impassible God does not suffer or perish), and NOT the Father or the Spirit (the ancient error of patripassianism). The one saving work stays undivided; only the assumed humanity is the seat of suffering.

cards.q: Does asserting “one will” quietly pick a side against social Trinitarians?
cards.a: Apologia Daily reports, rather than adjudicates, the intramural debate between social and classical Trinitarians; both camps intend full Nicene orthodoxy. What this track affirms is the common floor: the persons are one God, distinguished by relation and not by rank — neither three separate beings nor mere aspects of one. But any account that makes each person a distinct centre of will and power crosses the line into tritheism.

obj.q: If the Son is begotten and the Spirit proceeds, they are FROM the Father — so the Father is the source and they are forever second. Derived deity is junior deity; the Arians just said it honestly: begotten means later, and later means lesser.
obj.model: This is precisely the inference Nicaea refused: the Son is “begotten, not made… God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God.” A relation of origin orders the persons without grading the essence — the Son receives not a portion or a lesser grade but the whole undivided divine nature, self-existence itself, given wholly. Derivation of person is not inequality of essence; the three are co-equal and co-eternal. Being from the Father is the Son’s glory, not his demotion; the radiance is exactly as old and exactly as bright as the flame. The persons are distinguished by order, never by rank.

obj.q: A relation cannot think, love, speak, or act — yet the persons plainly do all these. “Subsistent relation” is a category mistake dressed in Latin. But if you let each person be a full centre of consciousness and will to escape it, you have simply described three gods. Either too thin to be persons (modalism) or too thick to be one God (tritheism).
obj.model: The dilemma omits perichoresis. The one who thinks, loves, and acts is not a bare relation but the divine essence itself, subsisting as this relationally distinct person — acting in the one undivided operation and the one will that follow from the one nature, not as three separate minds (that would be tritheism). “Subsistent relation” names that, not an abstraction doing the acting. One thing must be conceded plainly, and not buried: we possess no positive model that makes the how transparent. The claim is only the more modest one — that no contradiction has been demonstrated. So the charge of incoherence does not succeed: the doctrine is a mystery, but it has not been shown to be a contradiction.

obj.q: Read as ordinary identity statements, the creed says the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Father is not the Son. By the transitivity of identity the Father must equal the Son. It is formally inconsistent unless “is God” quietly means something other than strict identity.
obj.model: Exactly so — and the rule of relations of origin was framed precisely to deny that “the Father is God” and “the Son is God” assert numerical identity between person and essence in a way that would make Father and Son identical to each other. The persons are not each identical to the divine essence as one thing is identical to another; they are the one essence subsisting in three relationally distinct ways. Aquinas anticipated the worry: in creatures relation is an accident added to a substance, but in God, who is utterly simple, the relation is the essence — really identical with it, yet really distinct from its opposing relation. Paternity and filiation are opposed relations, so the Father is genuinely not the Son; yet neither relation differs from the divine essence. The relations differ from each other without either differing from the essence they each are — the Father is distinct from the Son, but neither is distinct from the Godhead. That is an unusual logic, but it is not a contradiction, for the terms it holds together are not affirmed in the same respect.

obj.q: “Mutual indwelling” just pictures three beings so close they interpenetrate — but three-who-coinhere is still three. Perichoresis smuggles in a social committee and calls it one God.
obj.model: Mind the order of grounding. The persons are one God in virtue of the one undivided essence they wholly share; perichoresis manifests that unity and forbids the picture of three separate beings — it does not manufacture a oneness out of three that would otherwise stand apart. Nor does it collapse them: a thing cannot indwell itself, so indwelling presupposes real distinction. Perichoresis is the expression of a unity already grounded in the shared essence, not a substitute for it.

unseen.q: You say the three persons always act inseparably, as one agent. But only the Son died on the cross — the Father did not. So either your rule of inseparable operations is false, or the Father suffered and died on the cross too.
unseen.model: The rule holds, and the cross is where it shows its finest work, not where it breaks. Inseparable operation means the three act as one agent; it does not mean the effect is always shared identically. The whole Trinity works the one act of the incarnation — the one God unites human nature to himself — but the term of that one act, the person in whom human nature subsists, is proper to the Son alone. So the incarnate Son truly suffered and died on the cross in the human nature he assumed, and because only the Son became man, the cross is properly his — what he underwent in the flesh can be said of God the Son by virtue of the incarnation. What this does NOT say is that the divine nature itself suffered, weakened, or perished (the impassible God does not die), and it does NOT say that the Father or the Spirit suffered — the ancient error of patripassianism. The one saving work stays undivided; only the assumed humanity is the seat of suffering. The undivided act simply has a personally distinct terminus — and naming that correctly is one of the doctrine’s finest achievements, not an embarrassment to it.
